items.title: The Futures Field: Functions, Forms, and Critical Issues
items.why: A classic reference for the basic orientation of futures studies around possible, probable, and preferable futures. It gives useful background for why futures research is not simple prediction.

items.title: Causal Layered Analysis: Poststructuralism as Method
items.why: One of the central methodological texts in futures studies. It is important for thinking about layers of futures: litany, systems, worldview, and myth/metaphor.

items.title: Foundations of Futures Studies
items.why: A broad foundation for futures studies as a field. It is useful when asking what kind of knowledge, judgement, and responsibility futures research can have.

items.title: An outline of future-oriented dialectics
items.why: A relevant conceptual paper for thinking about trajectories, tensions, and dialectical positions in futures research. It connects well with work that treats opposed futures as productive material.

items.title: Techniques of futuring: On how imagined futures become socially performative
items.authors: Jasper Oomen, Jesse Hoffman & Maarten A. Hajer
items.why: Useful for understanding futures not only as images, but as practices and techniques that can shape social reality.

items.title: Does the intuitive logics method – and its recent enhancements – produce effective scenarios?
items.authors: George Wright, Ron Bradfield & George Cairns
items.why: A useful quality discussion for scenario methods. It belongs to the methodological background for asking what makes scenario work actually helpful.

items.title: The critical role of history in scenario thinking
items.authors: Ron Bradfield, James Derbyshire & George Wright
items.why: A strong bridge between historical reasoning and scenario work. It is relevant for thinking about how the past can help causal analysis of the future without assuming repetition.

items.title: Unifying weak signals definitions to improve construct understanding
items.authors: B. L. van Veen & J. R. Ortt
items.why: Relevant for horizon scanning because it clarifies a frequently used but often unclear concept. A scan needs concepts that are not too loose.

items.title: Introduction to narrative for futures studies
items.why: A useful entry point for understanding what narrative can do in futures studies and why narrative is more than decoration for scenarios.

items.title: Narrative foresight
items.why: A central paper for narrative foresight. It helps explain why futures are not only analysed but also told, negotiated, and lived through stories.

items.title: Creating narrative scenarios: Science fiction prototyping at Emerge
items.why: Shows how narrative scenario work and science fiction prototyping can make futures more concrete and discussable.

items.title: Futures literacy through narrative
items.authors: Genevieve Liveley, William Slocombe & Emily Spiers
items.why: Connects narrative with futures literacy. It is helpful for thinking about how people learn to work with futures through story, temporality, and imagination.

items.title: Futures in Action: Expectations, Imaginaries and Narratives of the Future
items.why: Useful for understanding how futures, imaginaries, expectations, and narratives shape action. It gives a social-theoretical neighbour to narrative foresight.

items.title: Leadership in the Imagination Age: Navigating Unprecedented Possibilities and Moral Challenges
items.why: A useful bridge between leadership, imagination, storytelling, ethics, systems thinking, and futures studies. I placed it in Narrative foresight because its strongest radar value is how it treats leadership as orientation, moral imagination, and world-shaping storytelling under uncertainty.

items.title: The Delphi Method: Techniques and Applications
items.why: A foundational volume for Delphi as a method tradition. It gives historical and methodological background for more specific Delphi designs.

items.title: Disaggregative policy Delphi: Using cluster analysis as a tool for systematic scenario formation
items.why: A major example of developing Delphi beyond simple consensus. It is useful background for seeing how Delphi can handle plural viewpoints.

items.title: The Delphi technique: Past, present, and future prospects — Introduction to the special issue
items.why: A compact overview of Delphi as a continuing methodological tradition, useful for locating new Delphi variants inside the wider field.

items.title: Review of Delphi-based scenario studies: Quality and design considerations
items.authors: Markus Nowack, Jan Endrikat & Edeltraud Guenther
items.why: A useful methodological review for how Delphi and scenario work have been combined, and what quality problems need attention.

items.title: Improving the Delphi process: Lessons from social psychological research
items.why: Helpful for improving Delphi design through attention to judgement, group processes, and expert reasoning.

items.title: Consensus measurement in Delphi studies: Review and implications for future quality assurance
items.why: Important for the usual consensus-oriented side of Delphi. It is also useful when contrasting consensus with disagreement, tension, and dialectic designs.

items.topic: Philosophy of science and futures of science
items.title: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions
items.why: Still central for thinking about paradigms, scientific change, normal science, and rupture. It is unavoidable background for futures of science.

items.topic: Philosophy of science and futures of science
items.title: Representing and Intervening
items.why: Important for philosophy of science because it shifts attention to intervention, experiment, and scientific practice, not only representation.

items.topic: Philosophy of science and futures of science
items.title: Scientific Realism: How Science Tracks Truth
items.why: A central defence of scientific realism. It matters for futures of science because assumptions about continuity and truth shape how scientific futures are imagined.

items.title: Exceeding Our Grasp: Science, History, and the Problem of Unconceived Alternatives
items.why: Central for thinking about unconceived alternatives and the limits of our ability to imagine serious alternatives to present theories or worlds.

items.title: Darwin Deleted: Imagining a World without Darwin
items.why: A substantial example of counterfactual history of science. It helps show how alternative histories can illuminate what did and did not depend on a single figure.

items.title: Science As It Could Have Been
items.authors: Léna Soler, Emiliano Trizio & Andrew Pickering (eds.)
items.why: A major collection on contingency and inevitability in science. It gives background for asking how different science could have been.

items.title: So close no matter how far: counterfactuals in history of science and the inevitability/contingency controversy
items.why: Important for the problem that counterfactual histories may be pulled back toward the actual present. It is highly relevant for limits of conceivability.

items.title: Building futures scenarios for universities and higher education: An international approach
items.why: Useful for the methodological tradition of thinking about universities through scenarios and international comparison.

items.title: Visioning 2035: The future of the higher education sector in the UK
items.authors: Eddie Blass, Anne Jasman & Steve Shelley
items.why: A useful scenario-oriented paper on higher education futures. It gives background for comparing institutional futures over a long horizon.

items.title: The third mission of the university: A systematic literature review on potentials and constraints
items.why: Useful for university futures because it examines the third mission and the tensions around social, economic, and institutional roles of universities.

items.title: Only connect: Designing university futures
items.why: A recent and relevant piece for thinking about university futures with philosophical and institutional seriousness.

items.title: Augmentation or automation? The expanding role of artificial intelligence in urban planning and governance
items.authors: Frank Othengrafen, Lars Sievers, Merle Frankl
items.source: International Journal of Urban Sustainable Development. DOI: 10.1080/19463138.2026.2686016
items.why: Relevant as an empirical Delphi-based study of how AI is being positioned in urban planning and governance, especially the distinction between decision-support augmentation and automation.

items.title: Spatial implications of remote work: insights from seven European case studies
items.authors: Georgia Pozoukidou, Theodora Istoriou, Dimitra Plastara, Margarita Angelidou, Katharina Fellnhofer et al.
items.why: Useful for the futures-of-work strand because it treats remote work as a spatial and governance issue rather than only an individual employment preference.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in strategic foresight: Evidence from a longitudinal case at Siemens Professional Education
items.authors: René Rohrbeck, Stephan Szuppa & Julia Schmidt
items.why: Relevant to the futures-of-work strand because it examines how AI-augmented foresight is used to anticipate future skill requirements and support education and reskilling decisions, while showing key trade-offs in human–AI collaboration.

items.title: Three theses of the future as a Science, Technology and Society Studies research object: current approaches and challenges
items.authors: Cristián Navarrete, Iván Ojeda-Pereira, Fernando Campos-Medina, Sebastián Herrera-León
items.source: Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. DOI: 10.1057/s41599-026-07541-0
items.why: A strong conceptual fit for the radar because it treats the future itself as an STS research object and connects futures studies with science and technology studies.

items.title: Is the futures studies community thriving together? – A bibliometric approach
items.source: European Journal of Futures Research, 14, Article 17. DOI: 10.1186/s40309-026-00281-z
items.why: A useful empirical self-examination of futures studies as a research community. The bibliometric analysis tracks publication growth, co-publication, connectedness, and international cooperation across the field.

items.title: Governance logics and foresight functions: European strategic foresight in contrastive perspective
items.source: European Journal of Futures Research. DOI: 10.1186/s40309-026-00278-8
items.why: Shows that foresight methods are not merely transferable tools but are embedded in governance settings and perform different institutional functions. The contrastive European perspective is useful for analysing how strategic foresight changes across policy and administrative contexts.

items.title: How and when remote workdays impact employee daily social need fulfilment
items.authors: Vera M. Schweitzer, Anne Burmeister, Laura Venz, Fabiola H. Gerpott, Ulrike Fasbender et al.
items.source: Journal of Occupational and Organizational Psychology. DOI: 10.1111/joop.70150
items.why: Provides a focused empirical contribution to the futures of hybrid work by examining how and under what conditions remote workdays affect employees’ daily social need fulfilment. It is useful for thinking about work arrangements beyond productivity alone.

items.title: Foresight on spatial mobility during green and digital transitions: insights from five European regions
items.authors: Anastasia Panori, Natalia Głowacka & Asya Salnikova
items.why: Connects regional foresight and scenario work with the changing spatial mobility implications of green and digital transitions. Its comparative evidence from five European regions makes it relevant to policy-oriented, stakeholder-based foresight at the territorial level.

items.title: Beyond the Binaries: Techno-Optimism and Pessimism as Situated Epistemic-Affective Orientations
items.why: A useful contribution to debates about technological futures because it treats techno-optimism and pessimism as situated epistemic-affective orientations rather than simple opposing positions. It is especially relevant for analysing how anticipation, uncertainty, knowledge, and critique acquire normative force.

items.title: Anticipatory governance and leadership for AI implementation in higher education: A scoping review
items.source: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. DOI: 10.1186/s41239-026-00616-7
items.why: Directly relevant to university futures because it reviews how anticipatory governance and leadership are conceptualised and operationalised for AI-related transformation in higher education. The system- and organisational-level focus makes it useful for connecting foresight with institutional governance and implementation.

items.title: Wargames Are Experiments: Wargames as Experimental Methods in International Relations
items.source: Zeitschrift für Außen- und Sicherheitspolitik. DOI: 10.1007/s12399-026-01107-3
items.why: Relevant to the counterfactual strand because it examines wargames as experimental methods for testing causal hypotheses, exploring counterfactual scenarios, and generating evidence about decision-making. Its attention to design conditions and epistemological limits makes it useful for thinking about what scenario-based experiments can establish.

items.title: The generation of scientific knowledge in futures studies and foresight
items.why: A rare recent attempt to state what would make futures studies epistemically reliable without reducing reliability to predictive success. Its use of social reliabilism makes it directly relevant to questions about evidence, scientific legitimacy, and the standards by which futures claims should be judged.

items.title: Cognitive mechanisms in foresight: A bridge between psychology and futures studies
items.why: A useful bridge between foresight practice and cognitive science. It identifies memory, creativity, emotion, bias, and group processes as mechanisms that shape what people can generate and judge as futures, giving a firmer basis for evaluating participatory foresight.

items.title: Regimes of futurity: Progress, catastrophe, and historicity in the Anthropocene
items.why: A conceptually serious paper on the historical forms through which societies relate to the future. It is valuable for resisting the assumption that 'the future' is a stable object and for connecting futures studies with historicity, progress, catastrophe, and the Anthropocene.

items.title: Types of scenario planning and their effectiveness: A review of reviews
items.authors: Kathya Cordova-Pozo & Etiënne A. J. A. Rouwette
items.why: One of the strongest recent attempts to impose order on the methodological diversity of scenario planning. It synthesizes review evidence on definitions, schools, techniques, and effectiveness rather than treating scenario practice as self-validating.

items.title: Enhancing the horizon scanning utility of futures-oriented systematic and scoping reviews
items.authors: Eray Arda Akartuna, Shane D. Johnson & Amy Thornton
items.why: A concrete methodological contribution to horizon scanning that connects scanning with systematic review practice and explicit quality appraisal. The proposed neutrality-evidence-relevance-clarity framework is especially useful for distinguishing signals from low-quality noise.

items.title: Developments and challenges of foresight evaluation: Review of the past 30 years of research
items.why: Evaluation is one of the weakest parts of foresight methodology. This review maps three decades of work on how foresight quality and impact have actually been assessed, making it useful for judging methods by more than process elegance or participant satisfaction.

items.title: Anticipating futures: Understanding the fundamental importance of narratives through an integrative interdisciplinary approach
items.why: A broad interdisciplinary argument for treating narratives as dynamic components of anticipation rather than decorative communication. It connects empirical-analytical, narrative-experiential, and socio-technological approaches and emphasizes how narratives evolve through feedback and engagement.

items.title: Literary futures: Harnessing fiction for futures work
items.authors: Rebecca Braun, Orla Lehane & Maria Roca Lizarazu
items.why: A particularly well-developed recent attempt to turn literary technique into a research-informed futures method. Its use of character, worldbuilding, and participant evidence makes it stronger than generic claims that fiction merely stimulates imagination.

items.title: Exploring cultural futures: Dimensions of projectivity as a methodological lens for narrative analysis
items.why: A methodologically useful application of Mische's dimensions of projectivity to future-oriented narratives. It gives narrative analysis explicit dimensions—such as reach, contingency, connectivity, and volition—instead of treating stories as unanalyzed wholes.

items.title: Proposal for a critical appraisal tool for studies using the Delphi method (DCAT)
items.why: A major methodological contribution because it turns general complaints about Delphi quality into an explicit appraisal instrument. The 16-item DCAT provides a basis for judging design, data collection, analysis, and reporting across Delphi studies.

items.title: Biases in expert judgements in large-scale S&T Delphi Surveys: How to cope with them?
items.authors: Alexander Sokolov, Anna Grebenyuk & Kuniko Urashima
items.why: Important empirical evidence against the assumption that additional Delphi rounds naturally improve judgments through convergence. By comparing major national S&T Delphi exercises, it identifies systematic biases and shows why iteration itself cannot be treated as a quality guarantee.

items.title: Evaluating Delphi survey accuracy in transportation: Evidence from Japanese technology foresight
items.authors: Sukhayl Niyazov, Olesia Maibakh, Alexei Sukharev, Tatiana Kulakova & Andrey Ufimtsev
items.why: Unusually valuable because it evaluates Delphi forecasts against what later happened. The paper directly tests accuracy across 167 technology topics and also questions whether a second Delphi round improves forecasting performance.

items.topic: Philosophy of science and futures of science
items.title: Artificial intelligence tools expand scientists’ impact but contract science’s focus
items.authors: Qianyue Hao, Fengli Xu, Yong Li et al.
items.why: A large-scale empirical result with direct implications for the future organization of science: AI use is associated with greater individual scientific impact while scientific attention becomes more concentrated. It raises a fundamental tension between productivity and epistemic diversity.

items.topic: Philosophy of science and futures of science
items.title: The Interplay of Data, Models, and Theories in Machine Learning
items.authors: Maria Federica Norelli, Ioannis Votsis & Jon Williamson
items.why: A direct philosophy-of-science intervention into how machine-learning models relate to data and theory. It is useful for thinking beyond the simplistic idea that AI is either a black-box tool or a replacement for theory.

items.topic: Philosophy of science and futures of science
items.title: Can Generative AI Produce Novel Evidence?
items.why: A sharp conceptual paper on a genuinely new epistemic question: whether generative AI outputs can count as evidence rather than merely representations or hypotheses. Its historical-science cases make the issue concrete and relevant to changing scientific practice.

items.title: Historical contingency and counterfactual history: Revisiting the Cushing thesis
items.source: Studies in History and Philosophy of Science, 119, 102235
items.why: A very recent, careful test of one of the best-known counterfactual histories of science. It shows how apparent plausibility can depend on stripping away precisely the contextual contingencies that a serious counterfactual history needs to preserve.

items.title: When to Use Counterfactuals in Causal Historiography: Methods for Semantics and Inference
items.why: A method-focused account of when counterfactual reasoning genuinely helps causal historical inquiry. It connects interventionist causation with problems of variable specification, contrast classes, and inference instead of defending counterfactual history in the abstract.

items.title: Causes, Counterfactuals, and Counterfactual History
items.source: Journal of the Philosophy of History, 20(2), 133–155
items.why: A useful conceptual separation of different counterfactual roles in causal inquiry and historical speculation. It identifies where counterfactual reasoning becomes epistemically weak and proposes a more constrained methodology for counterfactual history.

items.title: Speculative futures for higher education
items.source: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 21, 39
items.why: A strong example of speculative method used reflexively rather than predictively. It treats higher-education futures as open and contested while showing how carefully designed speculative scenarios can support thought without pretending to forecast institutional outcomes.

items.title: Theorizing ‘the future’ in higher education: A framework for studying affective futurity
items.why: A sophisticated conceptual contribution that asks how university futures are not only imagined but felt. The framework of affective futurity links anticipation, hope, optimism, power, and social justice and expands university-futures research beyond institutional scenarios.

items.title: How universities study the future: A critical view
items.authors: Reza Hafezi, Sara Ghaboulian Zare, Firouzeh Rosa Taghikhah & Saeed Roshani
items.why: Directly relevant to the methodology of university-futures research. It critically reviews higher-education scenario studies rather than simply adding another scenario set, identifies recurring methodological weaknesses, and proposes guidance for stronger future work.

items.title: Generative AI at Work
items.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li & Lindsey Raymond
items.why: One of the strongest causal studies of generative AI in real work. Using data from 5,172 customer-support agents, it shows substantial average productivity effects but also strong heterogeneity by worker experience and skill, making it more informative than broad automation forecasts.

items.title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of Artificial Intelligence on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality
items.why: A foundational empirical paper for understanding AI and knowledge work because it shows that augmentation is task-dependent rather than uniform. The 'jagged technological frontier' gives a much better conceptual model than simple substitution-versus-complementarity claims.

items.title: The Cybernetic Teammate: A Field Experiment on Generative AI and Teamwork
items.why: A preregistered field experiment with professionals doing real product-innovation work. It examines not only output quality but expertise integration and social engagement, making it important for thinking about how AI may alter the structure and meaning of teamwork itself.
